An admirable sentiment, but there are numerous problems with this approach. First of all, it doesn't even address the underlying costs of college; it merely distributes the burden of paying tuition such that even people who don't go to college have to pay for it. Indeed, the move would likely raise the ultimate cost of a college education by eliminating competition: currently schools must compete for lower prices and students consider the expense when deciding which school to attend (I know I did personally). If school is "free"(read: paid instead through taxes which are out of sight and likely out of mind), the school's tuition is no longer part of the equation, removing any incentive to keep them as low as possible. The cost would be hidden, but it wouldn't go away, and would probably even increase.

Additionally, the proposal operates on the faulty premise that everyone should have a bachelor's degree. As many of us are learning the hard way, the job market is already saturated with college educated people who are finding out that having that those degrees, which sometimes had a $100,000+ price tag, aren't enough to get them jobs even within their chosen fields. Currently, the system is in the process of reacting (aptly) by shifting toward technical schools, apprenticeships, and other ways to give young people an edge with specific skills and knowledge that actually cost less money. We should if anything be encouraging this shift as a way to re-balance the job market, not discouraging it by footing the bills for all colleges.

Sanders is right that America needs to invest in education, but it needs to do so intelligently, not by simply throwing more money at it.
